explain.say: Today we look at Newton's three laws of motion. The first law describes inertia very well. Inertia is an object's resistance to changes in motion. An object at rest stays at rest unless a force acts on it. Think about a bus suddenly stopping. Your body continues moving forward due to inertia.

items: Inertia: Resistance to change in motion
At rest stays at rest unless force acts

draw.text: Inertia: Resistance to change in motion.

explain.say: Next we look at the second law, which is F equals m times a. This equation relates force, mass, and acceleration. The force applied equals the mass times the resulting acceleration. For example, if you push a small toy car, it accelerates easily. If you push a large truck, it accelerates much slower.

The third law is about action and reaction pairs. Whenever one object pushes another, the second object pushes back equally. This is the action and reaction pair. For instance, when you jump up, your feet push down on the ground. The ground pushes up on your feet with equal force.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. Weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass, measured in newtons. You have the same mass everywhere, but your weight changes on the Moon.
asks: Is weight the same as mass?
What units do I use for weight?

faq.q: Does the force have to be applied for an object to move?
faq.a: No, an object can move if a force is applied, but it can also move if it already has velocity. The first law explains that it keeps moving until a net force stops it.
asks: What stops motion if no force is applied?

faq.q: Are action and reaction forces always in the same direction?
faq.a: No, they are always equal in size but act on different objects. They act in opposite directions, which is key to understanding motion.
asks: Do action and reaction forces cancel out?

faq.q: If I double the force, what happens to the acceleration?
faq.a: If you double the force and keep the mass the same, the acceleration will also double. This is directly shown in the formula F equals m times a.
asks: If F increases, what happens to a?

faq.q: Does the second law apply to things floating in space?
faq.a: Yes, the second law still applies. Even in space, if you push something with a force, it will accelerate according to its mass.
asks: Can I use F=ma in space?

facts: Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion.
Newton's second law is mathematically expressed as Force equals mass times acceleration.
Newton's third law describes action and reaction forces acting on two different bodies.
The unit for force is the newton, and the unit for mass is the kilogram.

quiz.say: A passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly. This demonstrates:
quiz.why: The passenger's body tends to keep moving forward even when the bus stops.

wrong.0: This formula calculates the force needed, but the scenario describes the inherent property of the object.
wrong.1: While gravity is a force, the primary concept demonstrated by the lurching body is inertia.
wrong.3: This is tempting because forces are involved, but the main concept shown is resistance to change.

quiz.say: A rocket pushes gas downwards with a large force. The gas pushes the rocket upwards with:
quiz.why: Newton's third law states that the reaction force is always equal in size and opposite in direction.

wrong.0: While mass is involved, the direct relationship here is equality of force, not a calculation involving mass.
wrong.1: If there were no reaction force, the rocket would not move up.
wrong.3: The forces must be equal in magnitude according to the law.

quiz.say: If a net force of twenty newtons causes a five kilogram object to accelerate at four meters per second squared, what is the force?
quiz.why: Using F equals m times a, we calculate twenty newtons because five kilograms times four meters per second squared equals twenty newtons.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you multiply the mass by the acceleration twice.
wrong.1: This mistake happens if you only use the mass value in the calculation.
wrong.2: This assumes the object is at rest, ignoring the given acceleration.
